screens.title: Delegates and Events for Flexible Game Logic
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll see how C# delegates and events let different parts of a game talk to each other without tight coupling. Imagine a player picking up a coin: multiple systems need to react — score, sound, and messages — and delegates let the coin simply announce the collection while listeners respond. A delegate defines a method signature so that any matching method can be called through that delegate. An event wraps a delegate to enforce the publish-subscribe pattern: only the declaring class can invoke it, while others can only subscribe or unsubscribe. In Unity this leads to clearer, more maintainable code, and it prevents changes in one system from forcing edits across unrelated scripts. We'll walk through the classic PlayerHealth and UIManager examples, learn when to prefer static versus instance events, and see the critical OnEnable/OnDisable subscription pattern to avoid memory leaks. By the end you'll be able to design simple publisher classes and safe subscribers, apply Action and Func where appropriate, and diagnose common mistakes like forgetting to unsubscribe. Think about a time your game crashed from a callback — this lesson will show a cleaner pattern to avoid that outcome.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Delegates and Events

Delegates and Events

Learn the programmable callback types that let a publisher announce an occurrence and let multiple subscribers react without direct references.

In this lesson
Why delegates exist, how events wrap them, and Unity patterns to subscribe safely.
Coming up
PlayerHealth example, coin collection activity, and memory-leak avoidance.
Why it matters
Loose coupling makes your game easier to extend and maintain as systems grow.
Explore Key Topics
Delegate signatures
Define the method shape any handler must follow.
Events & safety
Events restrict who can invoke the callback list.
Subscription pattern
OnEnable and OnDisable keep subscriptions balanced to avoid leaks.
Visual Overview
Publisher
Declares an event and invokes it when something happens.
Subscribers
Subscribe with a matching method to react when invoked.
Key Takeaway

Delegates define signatures; events wrap them to provide controlled publish-subscribe behavior that reduces coupling and improves maintainability.

Quick code hint
public static event System.Action<int> OnCoinCollected; // event that passes coin value

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives prepare you to design loosely coupled game systems using delegates and events. First, you'll explain why delegates are useful for callback and event handling and how they improve maintainability. Second, you will implement custom delegates so you can define exact method signatures other systems must follow. Third, you'll create and use C# events to form a publish-subscribe pattern so publishers announce occurrences without knowing subscribers. Fourth, you'll practice differentiating delegates and events and learn when to use each. Each objective includes a concrete skill: reading a method signature, writing a delegate declaration, subscribing safely, and deciding static versus instance scope. Practically, you will see how a PlayerHealth publisher can notify a UI manager and a sound manager simultaneously without hard-coded references. A small misconception to avoid is treating events as simple variables; events restrict invocation rights, which is important for safe architecture. By mastering these objectives you reduce coupling, avoid brittle code changes, and design systems that scale as your game grows.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond understanding delegates and events, there are practical skills you must apply in Unity. First, know when to use the built-in Action and Func generic delegates to avoid writing custom types for common signatures. Second, practice choosing static events for global notifications and instance events for object-specific interactions; this choice affects lifetime and memory ownership. Third, be fluent in the OnEnable and OnDisable pattern: subscribe in OnEnable and always unsubscribe in OnDisable to avoid lingering references. Fourth, learn to use the null-conditional operator when invoking events so your code safely skips invocation if no listeners exist. These micro-skills keep your project stable as systems grow and they directly prevent common bugs like NullReferenceExceptions and memory leaks. Each micro-skill maps to a small verification you can try in the lab: add an Action event, subscribe and unsubscribe a manager, and observe no lingering references after object destruction. Practicing these patterns makes event-driven code predictable and easier to debug.

screens.title: Tight Coupling vs Loose Coupling
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining tight coupling: it is when one object directly calls methods on another and expects a concrete implementation. In simple projects this looks convenient — a coin directly calling a score manager and a sound manager — but as your project grows it becomes brittle. Any change to the called component can force changes in every caller. Loose coupling means components communicate through an agreed contract rather than direct calls. Delegates and events provide that contract in C#: they let a publisher announce something happened and let any matching subscriber respond. A concrete example: instead of Coin. FindAndCall( ui. UpdateScore ), declare an event OnCoinCollected that passes the coin value. ScoreManager and SoundManager subscribe to OnCoinCollected and react independently. This improves maintainability because adding a new response requires only subscribing a new handler, not editing existing code. A common misconception is thinking events only add indirection with no benefit — in practice the decoupling makes tests and refactors simpler. For a takeaway, ask: if you needed to add analytics on coin collection, would you edit the coin code or add a new subscriber? Loose coupling points to adding a subscriber every time.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Tight vs Loose Coupling
Definition

Tight coupling is direct dependence

When one script directly calls methods on another, changes ripple across callers and make maintenance harder.

Consequences
  • Harder to refactor or replace systems without touching callers.
  • More fragile tests and longer integration cycles.
  • Risk of runtime errors when objects are destroyed but still referenced.
Key Takeaway

Loose coupling via events prevents cascading code changes and lets you add behavior by subscribing instead of editing existing logic.

Concrete example

A Coin script should not call ScoreManager.Update directly. Instead publish OnCoinCollected and let ScoreManager subscribe. This way adding a MessageManager requires only subscribing.

Analogy

Think of a mailbox: the sender puts a note in and anyone who checks the mailbox can act. The sender doesn’t need to know who reads it.

Check your understanding

If you must add analytics for coin collection, which design requires fewer edits: direct calls or event subscription? Why?

screens.title: What Is a Delegate?
screens.narratorSegment: A delegate is a type that defines a method signature and can hold references to any method matching that signature. Think of it as a type-safe function pointer: it specifies parameter types and return type so the compiler enforces compatibility. This lets a variable of that delegate type reference different methods at runtime. For example, a custom delegate declaration like public delegate void OnPlayerDeath(string killerName) declares a shape for methods that take a string and return nothing. Any method matching that shape can be assigned and invoked via the delegate. Delegates aggregate multiple handlers: if several methods are added, invoking the delegate calls them all in sequence. A common practical use is callbacks for asynchronous or event-driven logic. A misconception is thinking delegates are the same as events — delegates are the underlying callable type, while events add access rules around them. When deciding between a custom delegate and using System. Action or System. Func, prefer Action or Func for common void or return-value signatures to keep code concise. For practice, try declaring a delegate for health-changed notifications and assign two handlers to observe the invocation order. What would happen if one handler throws an exception? Consider how that affects the chain and why safe invocation and error handling matter.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What Is a Delegate?
Formal definition

A type that encapsulates a method signature

Delegates let you store references to methods and later invoke them. The language enforces that signatures match.

Example delegate
// Custom delegate example
public delegate void OnPlayerDeath(string killerName);

Any method taking a string and returning void can be assigned to this delegate type.

Practical notes
  • Delegates can hold multiple handlers.
  • They are type-safe, preventing mismatched parameters at compile time.
  • Prefer built-in System.Action or System.Func when appropriate.
Misconception

Delegates are not events. Delegates are callable objects; events add access control around who can invoke them.

Key Takeaway

Use delegates to define the contract for callbacks; use Action/Func where possible for clarity.

screens.title: Delegates vs Events
screens.narratorSegment: Delegates and events are closely related but serve different roles. A delegate is the callable type: a variable of that type can be assigned and invoked from any code that has access. An event wraps a delegate and restricts invocation so that only the class declaring the event may invoke it. Subscribers can only add or remove handlers using += and -=. Practically, use a plain delegate when you need full control inside a class or in private APIs, but use events for public notification surfaces where you must prevent external code from clearing subscribers or invoking the list. For example, exposing public delegate PlayerDied on a class would allow outside code to overwrite the delegate or call it, creating instability. Exposing public event PlayerDied instead ensures only the publisher calls it. Another important contrast is that events enforce the publish-subscribe pattern and make intent clear in the A P I. A common pitfall is treating events as a way to store global state; remember they are notification channels, not storage. To practice, try converting a public delegate to a public event and observe how invocation must be restricted to the declaring class. This leads to safer, more maintainable code in larger projects.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Delegates vs Events
Delegate

Callable type

A variable of a delegate type can be directly invoked and reassigned by any code with access to it, making it flexible but less safe for public APIs.

When to use

Internal APIs or private callback stores where full control is required.

Event

Controlled publisher

An event allows external code to subscribe or unsubscribe but only the declaring class can invoke, preventing accidental external invocation or clearing.

When to use

Public notifications like OnPlayerDied or OnHealthChanged that many parts of the game may observe.

Quick practice

Change a public delegate to an event and ensure only the publisher invokes it. Notice the API now prevents external invocation.

Common mistake

Exposing a delegate publicly lets other code overwrite the handler list; prefer events for public notifications.

screens.title: PlayerHealth — Publishing events
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a PlayerHealth example that declares events other systems can subscribe to. The PlayerHealth class uses Action for health changes and Action for death notifications. It keeps a private current health value and, when damage is applied, it clamps health and then invokes OnHealthChanged with the new value. The code uses the null-conditional operator when invoking events to skip invocation if there are no subscribers. When health reaches zero, the Die method invokes OnPlayerDied and disables the player GameObject. This pattern isolates the publisher: PlayerHealth does not know who listens or what they do. A concrete benefit is that UI or sound systems can subscribe without the player class managing them. One subtle issue: static events persist beyond any single instance lifetime, so prefer instance events when the event should belong to a particular object. Also handle exceptions in subscriber code — a single throwing subscriber can disrupt the chain. Practice reading the code and confirming where subscriptions would occur elsewhere. After you study the snippet, ask: if there are no subscribers, will invoking OnHealthChanged cause an exception? The null-conditional invoke guards against that, keeping the game stable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › PlayerHealth Example
PlayerHealth.cs (publisher)
using UnityEngine;
using System;

public class PlayerHealth : MonoBehaviour
{
  public int MaxHealth = 100;
  private int _currentHealth;

  public static event Action<int> OnHealthChanged;
  public static event Action OnPlayerDied;

  void Awake() { _currentHealth = MaxHealth; }

  public void TakeDamage(int amount)
  {
    _currentHealth -= amount;
    _currentHealth = Mathf.Max(0, _currentHealth);
    OnHealthChanged?.Invoke(_currentHealth);
    if (_currentHealth <= 0) Die();
  }

  private void Die()
  {
    OnPlayerDied?.Invoke();
    gameObject.SetActive(false);
  }

  public void RestoreHealth(int amount)
  {
    _currentHealth += amount;
    _currentHealth = Mathf.Min(MaxHealth, _currentHealth);
    OnHealthChanged?.Invoke(_currentHealth);
  }
}
Explanation and notes
  • OnHealthChanged is an event that passes current health as an int.
  • OnPlayerDied is a simple notification without parameters.
  • The null-conditional invoke prevents exceptions when there are no subscribers.
  • Disabling the player in Die prevents further input and signals end-of-life to subscribers.
Pro tip

Decide whether events should be static or instance based on whether messages are global or per-object.

screens.title: UIManager — Subscribing and Unsubscribing
screens.narratorSegment: Now consider a subscriber like UIManager that updates health text and shows a game over panel. The correct pattern is to subscribe in OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable so event handlers do not survive the subscriber’s lifecycle. If you subscribe without unsubscribing, the event keeps a reference to the destroyed object and prevents garbage collection, causing a memory leak and potentially a NullReferenceException when the event later tries to call the handler. UIManager example shows subscribing to PlayerHealth. OnHealthChanged and PlayerHealth. OnPlayerDied in OnEnable, and removing them in OnDisable. This pattern is straightforward but critical. A common confusion is thinking Unity automatically cleans these references — it does not. Another subtlety: if you subscribe in Start, you must still unsubscribe appropriately, and if scripts enable/disable frequently, OnEnable/OnDisable is the most reliable place. After reading the code, try destroying the UI object and invoking the event; if you unsubscribed correctly nothing should be called and no exceptions occur. The takeaway: pair every += with a -= during the same lifecycle window. UIManager — Subscribing and Unsubscribing means always pair subscription and unsubscription within the component lifecycle to prevent memory leaks and runtime errors.. In practical terms, use onenable and ondisable to avoid memory leaks and invalid callbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › UIManager Subscription
UIManager.cs (subscriber)
using UnityEngine;
using TMPro;

public class UIManager : MonoBehaviour
{
  public TextMeshProUGUI healthText;
  public GameObject gameOverPanel;

  void OnEnable()
  {
    PlayerHealth.OnHealthChanged += UpdateHealthDisplay;
    PlayerHealth.OnPlayerDied += ShowGameOverScreen;
  }

  void OnDisable()
  {
    PlayerHealth.OnHealthChanged -= UpdateHealthDisplay;
    PlayerHealth.OnPlayerDied -= ShowGameOverScreen;
  }

  void Start() { gameOverPanel.SetActive(false); }

  void UpdateHealthDisplay(int currentHealth)
  {
    if (healthText != null) healthText.text = $"Health: {currentHealth}";
  }

  void ShowGameOverScreen()
  {
    if (gameOverPanel != null) gameOverPanel.SetActive(true);
    Debug.Log("Game Over UI displayed!");
  }
}
Why it matters
  • Unsubscribing prevents the event from holding references to destroyed objects.
  • Proper pairing avoids memory leaks and NullReferenceExceptions when events fire later.
  • OnEnable/OnDisable is safer than Start/OnDestroy for frequently enabled components.
Common mistake

Forgetting -= causes the event to hold a dangling reference, which blocks garbage collection and causes unpredictable callbacks.

screens.title: Coin Collection — Implementing a Publish-Subscribe Flow
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity demonstrates the publish-subscribe flow with a coin. The Coin script declares a static event OnCoinCollected that passes an integer coin value. When the player collects the coin, Coin invokes the event and destroys itself. A ScoreManager subscribes to the event in OnEnable and increments a private score, then unsubscribes in OnDisable. A SoundManager also subscribes and plays a coin sound (simulated by a console message). This pattern shows how one trigger can fan out to multiple independent reactions without the coin needing direct references to score or sound systems. A common question is whether events should be static: static events are suitable for simple global messaging, but be mindful they persist across scenes and can hold references longer than expected. Another concern is testing: with events, you can simulate collection by invoking a simulated method to ensure subscribers respond. Practically, implement these three scripts in your project, run collection, and watch console logs for score updates and sound messages. The key practice is pairing every subscription with an unsubscribe to keep memory clean as objects are created and destroyed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Coin Collection Activity
Coin.cs (publisher)
using UnityEngine;
using System;

public class Coin : MonoBehaviour
{
  public int coinValue = 10;
  public static event Action<int> OnCoinCollected;

  void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
  {
    if (other.CompareTag("Player"))
    {
      Debug.Log($"Player collected a coin worth {coinValue}!");
      OnCoinCollected?.Invoke(coinValue);
      Destroy(gameObject);
    }
  }

  public void SimulateCollection()
  {
    Debug.Log($"Simulating collection of a coin worth {coinValue}!");
    OnCoinCollected?.Invoke(coinValue);
    Destroy(gameObject);
  }
}
ScoreManager.cs (subscriber)
using UnityEngine;

public class ScoreManager : MonoBehaviour
{
  private int _currentScore = 0;

  void OnEnable() { Coin.OnCoinCollected += AddScore; }
  void OnDisable() { Coin.OnCoinCollected -= AddScore; }

  void AddScore(int value)
  {
    _currentScore += value;
    Debug.Log($"Current Score: {_currentScore}");
  }
}
Activity steps
  1. Create Coin, ScoreManager, and SoundManager scripts and attach them to GameObjects.
  2. Implement the static event in Coin and invoke it on collection.
  3. Subscribe in OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable in subscribers.
  4. Run the scene, collect a coin, and observe logs for score and sound outputs.
Key Takeaway

One publisher can notify many subscribers and adding behavior requires only subscribing, not editing the publisher.

screens.title: Subscription Lifecycle and Memory Management
screens.narratorSegment: Managing the lifecycle of subscriptions is essential. The usual process is: declare the event in the publisher, subscribe handlers in the subscriber's OnEnable, unsubscribe them in OnDisable, and prefer instance events unless the message is truly global. Step one: decide event scope — instance events belong to a specific object and will be garbage-collected when the object is collected; static events live across instances and can cause lingering references if subscribers are not removed. Step two: subscribe in OnEnable to ensure a handler is active when the component becomes active. Step three: unsubscribe in OnDisable to remove the reference and allow the subscriber to be collected. Step four: invoke with the null-conditional operator to avoid exceptions when there are no listeners. A concrete example: ScoreManager subscribing to Coin. OnCoinCollected must unsubscribe in OnDisable; otherwise the static event will keep the ScoreManager alive. A common misconception is that destroying a GameObject removes its subscriptions automatically — it does not. The takeaway: always pair every += with a -= and choose static events only when necessary for global messaging, otherwise prefer instance events to align lifetimes naturally.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Subscription Lifecycle

Four-step process to manage events

1. Decide scope
Use static for global events, instance for per-object events.
2. Subscribe
Subscribe handlers in OnEnable so they activate with the component.
3. Unsubscribe
Unsubscribe in OnDisable to remove references and allow GC to collect.
4. Safe invoke
Use ?.Invoke() to avoid calling when there are no listeners.
Key Takeaway

Pair every subscription with an unsubscribe and align event scope with object lifetime to prevent memory leaks and runtime errors.

screens.title: Debugging Event Issues and Memory Leaks
screens.narratorSegment: When events misbehave, two recurring issues appear: NullReferenceExceptions when invoking events without guards, and memory leaks due to unsubscribed handlers. NullReferenceExceptions occur when you invoke a delegate that is null because no subscriber exists. The idiomatic fix is to use the null-conditional operator, for example OnHealthChanged?. Invoke(value). Memory leaks happen when an event holds a reference to a destroyed MonoBehaviour because the subscriber never unsubscribed. The symptom is that objects you thought discarded remain in memory or cause callbacks when they should not. To debug, search for += usage and verify the corresponding -= is in OnDisable or OnDestroy. Use logs to confirm unsubscribes occur, and consider adding unit tests that create and destroy subscribers to assert no lingering references. Another debugging tip is to temporarily remove subscribers and invoke the event to see which handlers throw exceptions; wrap subscriber bodies in try-catch if a single failure should not break the chain. Finally, be mindful of static events across scenes: they persist, so clear or reinitialize them when appropriate. The main lesson is: follow lifecycle patterns and guard invocations to keep event-driven systems reliable.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Debugging Events
Symptoms and fixes
  • NullReferenceException when invoking: use ?.Invoke() to guard calls.
  • Memory leak after object destroyed: ensure you unsubscribe in OnDisable or OnDestroy.
  • Unexpected callbacks from destroyed objects: check static events are cleared.
Debug tip

Log subscription and unsubscription calls, and write small tests that create and destroy subscribers to confirm no lingering references remain.

Example guard
// Safe invocation
OnHealthChanged?.Invoke(currentHealth);
Common pitfall

Relying on object destruction to clear subscriptions without explicit -= leaves hard-to-find memory leaks.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll see how C# delegates and events let different parts of a game talk to each other without tight coupling. Imagine a player picking up a coin: multiple systems need to react — score, sound, and messages — and delegates let the coin simply announce the collection while listeners respond. A delegate defines a method signature so that any matching method can be called through that delegate. An event wraps a delegate to enforce the publish-subscribe pattern: only the declaring class can invoke it, while others can only subscribe or unsubscribe. In Unity this leads to clearer, more maintainable code, and it prevents changes in one system from forcing edits across unrelated scripts. We'll walk through the classic PlayerHealth and UIManager examples, learn when to prefer static versus instance events, and see the critical OnEnable/OnDisable subscription pattern to avoid memory leaks. By the end you'll be able to design simple publisher classes and safe subscribers, apply Action and Func where appropriate, and diagnose common mistakes like forgetting to unsubscribe. Think about a time your game crashed from a callback — this lesson will show a cleaner pattern to avoid that outcome.

These learning objectives prepare you to design loosely coupled game systems using delegates and events. First, you'll explain why delegates are useful for callback and event handling and how they improve maintainability. Second, you will implement custom delegates so you can define exact method signatures other systems must follow. Third, you'll create and use C# events to form a publish-subscribe pattern so publishers announce occurrences without knowing subscribers. Fourth, you'll practice differentiating delegates and events and learn when to use each. Each objective includes a concrete skill: reading a method signature, writing a delegate declaration, subscribing safely, and deciding static versus instance scope. Practically, you will see how a PlayerHealth publisher can notify a UI manager and a sound manager simultaneously without hard-coded references. A small misconception to avoid is treating events as simple variables; events restrict invocation rights, which is important for safe architecture. By mastering these objectives you reduce coupling, avoid brittle code changes, and design systems that scale as your game grows.

Beyond understanding delegates and events, there are practical skills you must apply in Unity. First, know when to use the built-in Action and Func generic delegates to avoid writing custom types for common signatures. Second, practice choosing static events for global notifications and instance events for object-specific interactions; this choice affects lifetime and memory ownership. Third, be fluent in the OnEnable and OnDisable pattern: subscribe in OnEnable and always unsubscribe in OnDisable to avoid lingering references. Fourth, learn to use the null-conditional operator when invoking events so your code safely skips invocation if no listeners exist. These micro-skills keep your project stable as systems grow and they directly prevent common bugs like NullReferenceExceptions and memory leaks. Each micro-skill maps to a small verification you can try in the lab: add an Action event, subscribe and unsubscribe a manager, and observe no lingering references after object destruction. Practicing these patterns makes event-driven code predictable and easier to debug.

Start by defining tight coupling: it is when one object directly calls methods on another and expects a concrete implementation. In simple projects this looks convenient — a coin directly calling a score manager and a sound manager — but as your project grows it becomes brittle. Any change to the called component can force changes in every caller. Loose coupling means components communicate through an agreed contract rather than direct calls. Delegates and events provide that contract in C#: they let a publisher announce something happened and let any matching subscriber respond. A concrete example: instead of Coin. FindAndCall( ui. UpdateScore ), declare an event OnCoinCollected that passes the coin value. ScoreManager and SoundManager subscribe to OnCoinCollected and react independently. This improves maintainability because adding a new response requires only subscribing a new handler, not editing existing code. A common misconception is thinking events only add indirection with no benefit — in practice the decoupling makes tests and refactors simpler. For a takeaway, ask: if you needed to add analytics on coin collection, would you edit the coin code or add a new subscriber? Loose coupling points to adding a subscriber every time.

A delegate is a type that defines a method signature and can hold references to any method matching that signature. Think of it as a type-safe function pointer: it specifies parameter types and return type so the compiler enforces compatibility. This lets a variable of that delegate type reference different methods at runtime. For example, a custom delegate declaration like public delegate void OnPlayerDeath(string killerName) declares a shape for methods that take a string and return nothing. Any method matching that shape can be assigned and invoked via the delegate. Delegates aggregate multiple handlers: if several methods are added, invoking the delegate calls them all in sequence. A common practical use is callbacks for asynchronous or event-driven logic. A misconception is thinking delegates are the same as events — delegates are the underlying callable type, while events add access rules around them. When deciding between a custom delegate and using System. Action or System. Func, prefer Action or Func for common void or return-value signatures to keep code concise. For practice, try declaring a delegate for health-changed notifications and assign two handlers to observe the invocation order. What would happen if one handler throws an exception? Consider how that affects the chain and why safe invocation and error handling matter.

Delegates and events are closely related but serve different roles. A delegate is the callable type: a variable of that type can be assigned and invoked from any code that has access. An event wraps a delegate and restricts invocation so that only the class declaring the event may invoke it. Subscribers can only add or remove handlers using += and -=. Practically, use a plain delegate when you need full control inside a class or in private APIs, but use events for public notification surfaces where you must prevent external code from clearing subscribers or invoking the list. For example, exposing public delegate PlayerDied on a class would allow outside code to overwrite the delegate or call it, creating instability. Exposing public event PlayerDied instead ensures only the publisher calls it. Another important contrast is that events enforce the publish-subscribe pattern and make intent clear in the A P I. A common pitfall is treating events as a way to store global state; remember they are notification channels, not storage. To practice, try converting a public delegate to a public event and observe how invocation must be restricted to the declaring class. This leads to safer, more maintainable code in larger projects.

Let's walk through a PlayerHealth example that declares events other systems can subscribe to. The PlayerHealth class uses Action for health changes and Action for death notifications. It keeps a private current health value and, when damage is applied, it clamps health and then invokes OnHealthChanged with the new value. The code uses the null-conditional operator when invoking events to skip invocation if there are no subscribers. When health reaches zero, the Die method invokes OnPlayerDied and disables the player GameObject. This pattern isolates the publisher: PlayerHealth does not know who listens or what they do. A concrete benefit is that UI or sound systems can subscribe without the player class managing them. One subtle issue: static events persist beyond any single instance lifetime, so prefer instance events when the event should belong to a particular object. Also handle exceptions in subscriber code — a single throwing subscriber can disrupt the chain. Practice reading the code and confirming where subscriptions would occur elsewhere. After you study the snippet, ask: if there are no subscribers, will invoking OnHealthChanged cause an exception? The null-conditional invoke guards against that, keeping the game stable.

Now consider a subscriber like UIManager that updates health text and shows a game over panel. The correct pattern is to subscribe in OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable so event handlers do not survive the subscriber’s lifecycle. If you subscribe without unsubscribing, the event keeps a reference to the destroyed object and prevents garbage collection, causing a memory leak and potentially a NullReferenceException when the event later tries to call the handler. UIManager example shows subscribing to PlayerHealth. OnHealthChanged and PlayerHealth. OnPlayerDied in OnEnable, and removing them in OnDisable. This pattern is straightforward but critical. A common confusion is thinking Unity automatically cleans these references — it does not. Another subtlety: if you subscribe in Start, you must still unsubscribe appropriately, and if scripts enable/disable frequently, OnEnable/OnDisable is the most reliable place. After reading the code, try destroying the UI object and invoking the event; if you unsubscribed correctly nothing should be called and no exceptions occur. The takeaway: pair every += with a -= during the same lifecycle window. UIManager — Subscribing and Unsubscribing means always pair subscription and unsubscription within the component lifecycle to prevent memory leaks and runtime errors.. In practical terms, use onenable and ondisable to avoid memory leaks and invalid callbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This hands-on activity demonstrates the publish-subscribe flow with a coin. The Coin script declares a static event OnCoinCollected that passes an integer coin value. When the player collects the coin, Coin invokes the event and destroys itself. A ScoreManager subscribes to the event in OnEnable and increments a private score, then unsubscribes in OnDisable. A SoundManager also subscribes and plays a coin sound (simulated by a console message). This pattern shows how one trigger can fan out to multiple independent reactions without the coin needing direct references to score or sound systems. A common question is whether events should be static: static events are suitable for simple global messaging, but be mindful they persist across scenes and can hold references longer than expected. Another concern is testing: with events, you can simulate collection by invoking a simulated method to ensure subscribers respond. Practically, implement these three scripts in your project, run collection, and watch console logs for score updates and sound messages. The key practice is pairing every subscription with an unsubscribe to keep memory clean as objects are created and destroyed.
